editorialDecl.p: EEBO-TCP is a partnership between the Universities of Michigan and Oxford and the publisher ProQuest to create accurately transcribed and encoded texts based on the image sets published by ProQuest via their Early English Books Online (EEBO) database (http://eebo.chadwyck.com). The general aim of EEBO-TCP is to encode one copy (usually the first edition) of every monographic English-language title published between 1473 and 1700 available in EEBO.

EEBO-TCP aimed to produce large quantities of textual data within the usual project restraints of time and funding, and therefore chose to create diplomatic transcriptions (as opposed to critical editions) with light-touch, mainly structural encoding based on the Text Encoding Initiative (http://www.tei-c.org).

The EEBO-TCP project was divided into two phases. The 25,363 texts created during Phase 1 of the project have been released into the public domain as of 1 January 2015. Anyone can now take and use these texts for their own purposes, but we respectfully request that due credit and attribution is given to their original source.
Users should be aware of the process of creating the TCP texts, and therefore of any assumptions that can be made about the data.

Text selection was based on the New Cambridge Bibliography of English Literature (NCBEL). If an author (or for an anonymous work, the title) appears in NCBEL, then their works are eligible for inclusion. Selection was intended to range over a wide variety of subject areas, to reflect the true nature of the print record of the period. In general, first editions of a works in English were prioritized, although there are a number of works in other languages, notably Latin and Welsh, included and sometimes a second or later edition of a work was chosen if there was a compelling reason to do so.

Image sets were sent to external keying companies for transcription and basic encoding. Quality assurance was then carried out by editorial teams in Oxford and Michigan. 5% (or 5 pages, whichever is the greater) of each text was proofread for accuracy and those which did not meet QA standards were returned to the keyers to be redone. After proofreading, the encoding was enhanced and/or corrected and characters marked as illegible were corrected where possible up to a limit of 100 instances per text. Any remaining illegibles were encoded as <gap>s. Understanding these processes should make clear that, while the overall quality of TCP data is very good, some errors will remain and some readable characters will be marked as illegible. Users should bear in mind that in all likelihood such instances will never have been looked at by a TCP editor.
The texts were encoded and linked to page images in accordance with level 4 of the TEI in Libraries guidelines.

Copies of the texts have been issued variously as SGML (TCP schema; ASCII text with mnemonic sdata character entities); displayable XML (TCP schema; characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or text strings within braces); or lossless XML (TEI P5, characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or TEI g elements).
Keying and markup guidelines are available at the Text Creation Partnership web site.
This file is the EEBO-TCP transcription with editorial layers added inline; nothing of the transcription has been removed.

choice/orig holds the text as printed; choice/reg holds the modern reading. reg/@resp says who decided it (#auto = machine, #editor = reviewed by hand); reg/@type is spelling, case, punctuation, spacing, grammar (an archaic form modernized: thou, hath, -eth) or emendation (another word, or a word added or removed). Where the editor overrode the machine, the editor's reg comes first and the machine's proposal follows as a second reg[@resp='#auto'].
choice/abbr + choice/expan: macron abbreviations (e.g. frō = from) and superscript contractions (yᵉ = the).
supplied: letters or words lost to illegible print, with @cert and a comment giving the evidence; the TCP gap element is kept inside.

Spelling regularized: u/v, i/j, silent final e, doubled consonants, -ie to -y, -nesse to -ness, and a word list. Grammatical forms (hath, doth, thou, thee, thy, ye, shalt, wilt, art, hast, dost) are retained. Footnote text is left in original spelling.
list[@change='#review']: run-in enumerations (I. ... II. ...) set out as numbered lists; the printed numerals are kept in label.
head[@type='edition']: section title used by this edition; the printed heading is kept in the preceding head. @change='#review' points at the revisionDesc entry for these structural changes.
Line breaks are those of the TCP transcription (newlines in the text; g[@ref='char:EOLhyphen'] marks a word hyphenated at line end). pb/@n is the printed page, pb/@facs the page image.
reg[@type='spacing']: a space this edition adds (empty orig) or removes (empty reg) between words.
@prev/@next link blocks this edition runs together into one paragraph; they stay separate elements as printed.
p[@rend='quote']: a paragraph this edition sets as a quotation.
@rend='run-on': a block this edition runs on from the one before without a space between them.
list/@rend: the numbering this edition gives a list (a Typst numbering pattern, e.g. 'a)'); item/@n on its first item: the number it starts from.
epigraph[@rend='quote']: a scripture epigraph this edition sets as a quotation in the text.

be accurſedaccursed, and they that dwell therein ſhallshall not drink Winewine with a Song, &csong..' Here you ſeesee all ſweetneſſesweetness and rejoycingrejoicing of heart is departed from them; yet even in the middeſtmidstmiddest of all theſethese miſeriesmiseries, God (, the God of comforts), makes ſweetsweet and gracious promiſespromises to his Churchchurch, to raiſeraise it out of its mournfullmournful eſtateestate and condition. And therefore the Prophetprophet, in the former part of this Chapterchapter, ſpeakesspeaks of bleſſingblessing God for the deſtructiondestruction of his Enemiesenemies, and for his great love to his Churchchurch. And when he had ſpokenspoken of the ruineruin of the enemieenemy, heehe preſentlypresently breaks out with ThankſgivingthanksgivingThanksgiving, breathing forth abundant praiſespraises to his God; as it is the cuſtomecustom of holy men (, guided by the motion of the bleſſedblessed Spirit of God, upon all occaſionsoccasions) (, but eſpeciallyespecially for benefits to his Churchchurch), to praiſepraise his Namename, not out of ill affection at the deſtructiondestruction of the AdverſariesadversariesAdversaries, but at the execution of Divine JuſticeJusticedivine justice, for the fulfilling of the truth of his promiſepromise; as in the firſtfirst VerſeverseVerse of this Chapterchapter;, O'O Lord, thou art my God,; I will exalt thee, I will praiſepraise thy name,; for thou haſthast done wonderfullwonderful things,; thy CounſelscounselsCounsels of old are faithfulneſſefaithfulness, and truth..' div.head: THE Ninth Sermon.

epigraph.q: And it ſhallshall be ſaidsaid in that day, loeLolo, this is our God,; weewe have waited for him, and he will ſavesave us: this is the Lord,; we have waited for him, we will be glad and rejoycerejoice in his ſalvationsalvation..—Isaiah 25:9.

div.p: INIn the worſtworst age of the Churchchurch, that the Churchchurch may not be ſwallowedswallowed up with fear, in the worſtworst times, God doth prepare promiſespromises for his people. It was the caſecase of our bleſſedblessed Saviour himſelfhimself to his poorepoor DiſciplesdisciplesDisciples, that they might not be overwhelmed with ſorrowsorrow. Wherein wherein we may conſiderconsider firſtfirst of all, Thatthat God hath left to his Churchchurch rich and precious promiſespromises, ſuchsuch as is ſpokenspoken of before.: Aa feaſtfeast, and removallremoval of all hinderanceshindrances whatſoeverwhatsoever. He not only vouchſafethvouchsafeth heaven when we dyedie, and eternalleternal happineſſehappiness,; but in this worldworld, in our wayway, he vouchſafesvouchsafes precious promiſespromises to ſupportsupport our faith, that we may begin heaven upon earth. What theſethese promiſespromises are, we ſhewedshowed the laſtlast day.

The ſecondsecond obſervationobservation was, in that GodsGod’s people are here in a ſtatestate of expectation., Itit ſhallshall be ſaidsaid, loe'Lo,lo we have waited for him..' Our eſtateestate here is a paſſagepassage to a better eſtateestate, and waiting is a diſpoſitiondisposition fit for ſuchsuch a condition.

And in this there is good, and imperfection;. goodGood, that we have ſomethingsomething to wait for,; imperfection, that we are to wait for it, that we have it not in fruition,; and till we be in heaven we are in a ſtatestate of waiting. In the Revelations, Come'Come, Lord JeſusJesus, come quicklyquickly,' Revelation 22:20, there is a glorious ſtatestate of a Churchchurch ſetset forth,; but while all is done, it hath not what it would have. The third thing is,Waiting not an empty thing. that as there be promiſespromises, and theſethese promiſespromises are not preſentlypresently fulfilled, which put us in a ſtatestate of waiting:, ſoso God giveth grace to uphold in waiting. We ſeesee in nature,Simile. Inin the winter, which is a dull time to the ſpringspring, and harveſtharvest, and the times are very cold; yet it ripens and mellowesmellows the ſoilesoil, and fits it for the ſpringspring. The gracious God that fits us for heaven,God fits heaven for us, and us for heaven. and heaven for us, fits us with all graces neceſſarynecessary for that condition. We are ſoso ſhortshort, even David and others,; and therefore God giveth grace to hold out and lengthen our ſpirituallspiritual faith, and hopehope, and perſeveranceperseverance, and conſtantconstant courage to encounter with all difficulties in the way. When the ſpiritspirit of a man beholds heaven, and happineshappiness, and God, it makes him conſtantconstant,constant in ſomesome ſortsort, as the things he beholdeth, for the ſpiritSpiritspirit transformeth him to the object. NowNow, he beholds a conſtantconstant Covenantcovenant:; Andand as faith looks upon a conſtantconstant God, conſtantconstant happineſſehappiness, and conſtantconstant promiſespromises, it frameth the ſoulesoul ſuitablesuitable to the excellency of the object it layeth hold upon.

And then the ſpiritSpiritspirit of God in the way to heaven, ſubduethsubdueth all evillevil murmurings, and exceptions, in ſufferingsuffering us not to put forth our hands to any iniquity,. thoughThough we have not what we would have, he keeps us in a good and fruitfullfruitful way; for to wait, is not only to endure, but
to endure in a good courſecourse, fitting us for happineſſehappiness, till grace end in glory.

In the fourth place, God will performeperform all his promiſespromises in time. As the Churchchurch ſaithsaith here, This'This is the Lord,; we have waited for him..' NowNow, he hath made good whatſoeverwhatsoever he hath ſaidsaid.

To inlargeenlarge this point a little.As there is a time of waiting, ſoso there will be a time of performing. As there is a time of waiting, ſoso there will be a time when GodsGod’s people ſhallshall ſaysay, Lee'Lo, this is the Lord, we have waited for him..' WhyWhy?

GodReason 1. God is Jehovah,. aA full and pregnant word,! aA word of comfort and ſtaystay for the ſoulesoul,1 ReaſReas. God is Jehovah. in this word Jehovah.!
